analysis.title: Nvidia Gets $690BN, The Other 499 Get $340BN: Tracing Every Dollar Of 2027's AI Capex
key_insights: Morgan Stanley's note 'Following AI's $1.6 trillion Money Trail' maps $1.58 trillion of 2027 hyperscaler and neocloud capex across nine buyers (Alphabet, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, a lease bucket, SpaceX, Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius) to single-stock supplier revenue. The capex maps to about $1.7 trillion of supplier revenue. MS attributes the gap to private neoclouds and bitcoin miners blurring the customer split, timing differences, and supplier price increases not yet in capex estimates.

AI capex is estimated to directly drive about 25% of S&P 500 sales growth in 2027 (24% by the article's own figure, up from 15% this year). AI enablers and adopters are estimated to account for 78% of 2027 S&P earnings growth.

MS adds $195 billion of lease-financed spending to 2027 capex and $246 billion to 2028, because leased data centers are economically the same as debt-funded capex but bypass the GAAP capex line. Total AI capex rises from $1.39 trillion in cash capex to $1.58 trillion in 2027 (about +60% YoY), and from $1.57 trillion to $1.81 trillion in 2028. 2026 capex roughly doubles to $978 billion.

Leases signed but not yet commenced total $1.118 trillion as of 2Q26, more than doubling in two quarters. Microsoft and Meta account for most of the signing. The article says SPVs, chip-collateralized loans and vendor backstops remain outside the $1.6 trillion.

About 65% of hyperscaler and neocloud capex is absorbed by S&P 500 companies, roughly $1.03 trillion or about 5% of index sales. That lifts S&P sales growth from 6.6% to 8.6%. Of the $1.03 trillion, 67% (about $690 billion, roughly 44% of the whole budget) lands on Nvidia. Excluding NVDA, AI capex is worth only 1.6% of S&P 500 sales.

The other 499 S&P names share roughly $340 billion. About $550 billion of the capex leaks outside the index to Korean memory makers, Taiwanese ODMs and private players. The article links this to a sharp KOSPI move this week.
Semis and servers are the largest bucket at $672 billion, mostly NVDA. 'International' suppliers (Samsung, SK hynix, Taiwan ODMs) are second at $511 billion and none are in the S&P.

Sector analysts estimate the share of 2027 revenue tied to AI infrastructure: Nvidia 91.7%, Erock (EROC) 91%, Vertiv 90%, Applied Opto 83%, Broadcom 81%, Bloom Energy 80%, Seagate and Western Digital 60% each, Caterpillar 21%. For these names a capex revision is an earnings revision with no other business to cushion it.

MS screened for pricing power from bottlenecks that should keep driving upward revisions as capex growth slows from +60% in 2027 to +14% in 2028. Power names (CAT, CMI, EROC, GEV, INIO, BE), memory, HDDs and the cooling group (VRT, TT, JCI) dominate.

42 S&P names classed 'Core to Thesis' AI enablers or adopters grow 2027 sales 28% vs 5% for everyone else and earnings 25% vs 4%. This cohort is 37% of index net income, with the Mag 7 contributing about three-quarters of its earnings.

Two caveats from MS on earnings. The ex-AI cohort's 4% growth is partly a base effect after 23% growth this year. The AI cohort's EPS growth peaked at 105% in 2Q26, skewed by private AI investment gains booked in non-operating profit, meaning part of this year's AI earnings growth came from hyperscalers marking up stakes in private AI labs.

MS's internet team (Brian Nowak) sees about 70 GW of capacity added in 2027/28 (32 GW and 38 GW), taking hyperscaler compute to about 125 GW by end-2028, 4x 2025. Custom ASICs rise from 34% of incremental capacity in 2025 to 66% by 2028, with 12 GW of Trainium and TPU vs 13 GW of Nvidia coming online in 2028. Nowak says 30-40% of 2026 capex goes into land, buildings and power for data centers opening 2027-2029.

MS models ROIC of about 31% for GPU rental, about 46% for a model API on owned infrastructure and about 25% on rented infrastructure. The base case assumes 75% utilization and token pricing of $1.75 per million. The article notes sensitivity to those two inputs is large.

Semis (Joe Moore): MS sees a $1 trillion accelerator market by 2028 and Nvidia revenue per GW above $50 billion on the Feynman platform. Moore calls NVDA the best risk/reward as the market questions 2027 AI capex, at 15x FY28 EPS. He would worry most 'at the tail of the bullwhip' (memory, optics, power management, analog) in a slowdown and warns there would be no safe havens in the sector.

Memory (Shawn Kim): Amazon's CFO attributed most of its capex increase (from about $200 billion to about $220 billion) to rising memory costs with no change to the build plan. MS concludes headline capex growth is partly a memory-price variable, so slower memory contract price growth into 4Q26 and 2027 would let hyperscalers report slower capex while building the same number of servers. Kim sees the memory cycle in its late stage by 4Q26, not ending, with memory stocks at about 3x NTM P/E.

Networking (Meta Marshall): each incremental dollar of hyperscaler capex has generated a stable share of networking revenue, so every $100 billion change in hyperscaler budgets moves annual networking revenue by about $15 billion. Names with the most hyperscaler exposure carry the most estimate risk.

Hardware and ODMs: MS forecasts Dell earning a roughly 5% gross margin on CY27 revenue from tier-2 CSPs and neoclouds, and Taiwan ODMs keep only a mid-single-digit share of rack ASP. Consensus has Big Four CSP capex growth slowing from about 90% this year to about 42% in 2027 and about 11% in 2028. Some hyperscalers already reported negative free cash flow in 2Q26.

Power equipment: GE Vernova gas turbines are sold out through 2029 and cost $3,000/kW vs $1,000/kW in the early 2020s. Power OEMs book orders out to 2032 and demand 20-40% deposits. Large-displacement engines are sold out through at least 1H28. MS flags industry turbine capacity heading toward about 150 GW a year vs about 50 GW in 2024, an oversupply risk.

Credit (Fernanda Lima, Vishwas Patkar): hyperscaler and neocloud free cash flow is expected to be most negative in 2027, more so including lease payments. Hyperscalers issued about $255 billion of unsecured bonds year-to-date (about 30% of estimated 2026 capex), led by Amazon and Alphabet, while all-in yields rose 100-180bp (Oracle's 10Y worst at +180bp).

MS's illustrative financing test: high-quality hyperscalers issuing $400 billion at 7% cuts interest coverage from 30.7x to 11.9x. Oracle and SpaceX issuing $120 billion at 8.5% cuts their combined coverage from 4.0x to 1.8x. MS distinguishes aggregate capital availability from individual borrowers' ability to access it on workable terms, a condition for delivering the capex estimates. Neoclouds rely almost entirely on debt.

MS expects the 2027 issuance mix to shift toward shorter-duration and asset-backed, chip-collateralized financing. The article notes Goldman and JPM refused to hold such structures on their own books at 11% this week, and cites a Goldman credit desk view that the AI unwind has entered phase two with a $106 billion debt bill due.

Upside risk: Wall Street has historically underestimated compute cycles (PC, internet, mobile, cloud) by an average of 38%. Downside risk: the 'fear of missing procurement' dynamic reverses once supply catches up. MS cites the 2022 memory downturn, when NAND shipments fell about 5% but prices fell 20-30%, and says the risk of volumes and prices falling together is underappreciated.

Power constraint: MS's Powering AI model shows a 32 GW net US shortfall through 2028 even after time-to-power solutions (34% of the 97 GW needed), widening to about 72 GW through 2029. MS frames it as a timing mismatch. Memory, networking, optical and ODM builds are most exposed to a pause and power-solution providers are relative winners.
Politics: MS's Ariana Salvatore notes no major midterm candidate is running as pro-data center 'without qualifiers' and tax breaks are the consensus target.

MS lays out two capex-slowdown scenarios (easing because returns are great, or because returns disappoint, leaving D&A and committed costs to drive earnings deleverage) and leans toward the former. The article leans toward the latter, or a third case where capex slows because debt funding runs out, arguing the binding constraint looks more like cost of capital than compute demand.

earnings_insights: MS estimates the 42 'Core to Thesis' AI S&P names grow 2027 sales 28% and earnings 25% (estimates, not reported), vs 5% and 4% for the rest of the index. The AI cohort would account for 78% of 2027 S&P 500 earnings growth.
AI cohort EPS growth peaked at 105% in 2Q26 (reported period), skewed by private AI investment gains in non-operating profit per MS.
S&P 500 2027 sales growth is estimated at 6.6% ex-AI and 8.6% with AI capex (MS forecast). Ex-AI earnings growth is 4% after 23% this year.
Amazon's CFO attributed most of the rise in 2026 capex from about $200 billion to about $220 billion to higher memory costs (company commentary as cited by MS).
MS forecasts Dell at roughly a 5% gross margin on CY27 revenue from tier-2 CSPs and neoclouds (forecast).
Forgent's data center business grew 161% last fiscal year (reported).

risk_factors: Financing: free cash flow turns most negative in 2027. Oracle and SpaceX combined interest coverage could fall from 4.0x to 1.8x on $120 billion of 8.5% debt, and neoclouds rely almost entirely on debt.
Volume and price falling together in a supply catch-up, as in the 2022 memory downturn (NAND shipments about -5%, prices -20-30%).
Power: a 32 GW net US shortfall through 2028 means ordered chips may not be powered and put to work.
Customer concentration: 67% of the index-level benefit goes to Nvidia, and custom ASICs rise to 66% of incremental capacity by 2028.
Part of headline capex growth is memory-price inflation rather than more servers.
Bullwhip over-ordering in small-dollar components (memory, optics, power management, analog) if demand slows.
Turbine oversupply: industry capacity heading to about 150 GW a year vs about 50 GW in 2024.
Private AI investment marks inflating 2026 AI earnings could reverse if private valuations fall.
Off-balance-sheet lease commitments over $1.1 trillion plus SPVs, chip-collateralized loans and vendor backstops sit outside the capex figure.

charts_described: Sankey diagram routing $1.58 trillion of 2027 spending by nine buyers (Alphabet, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, lease bucket, SpaceX, Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius) through semis and servers, networking and optical, data center infrastructure, US memory and storage and international suppliers to individual tickers, with a large NVDA flow in semis and servers.
vol_and_positioning: The AI cohort is 37% of S&P 500 net income and 78% of 2027 earnings growth, with the Mag 7 contributing about three-quarters of the cohort's earnings, a concentrated exposure.
At least a dozen large companies have 80%+ of 2027 revenue tied to AI infrastructure, so a capex revision becomes an earnings revision with no cushion.
Memory stocks trade at about 3x NTM P/E and the article says the memory complex was the epicenter of this month's AI selloff.
The article reports CoreWeave fell sharply on Wednesday, and that Anthropic IPO investors marked the valuation down to $1.5 trillion this week.
geopolitical: US midterm politics: MS notes no major candidate is running as pro-data center 'without qualifiers', and tax breaks for data centers are the consensus target.
Political backlash against data center buildouts is cited as one reason hyperscalers are building land, shell and power capacity early.
cross_bank_references: Goldman Sachs calculated how much revenue is needed to justify $1.7 trillion in hyperscaler capex (Sep 25), with a worst case of $920 billion a year just to cover depreciation and running costs.
Goldman's credit desk said this week the AI unwind has entered phase two as the $106 billion debt bill comes due.
Goldman and JPM refused to hold chip-collateralized structures on their own books at 11% this week, per the article.
Goldman's Delta One head also admitted that the binding constraint looks more like cost of capital than demand for compute, per the article.

tension_points.bull_case: MS argues AI capex lifts S&P sales growth from 6.6% to 8.6%, the index still grows without it, and Wall Street has historically underestimated compute cycles by an average of 38%. Capital intensity could ease because returns are great, with modeled ROIC of 25-46%.
tension_points.bear_case: The article and Goldman argue capex could slow because debt runs out. Free cash flow is most negative in 2027, Oracle and SpaceX coverage falls toward 1.8x, 67% of the index benefit goes to Nvidia, and 78% of earnings growth rides on one theme. A bearish MS scenario has capex easing because returns disappoint, leaving D&A and committed costs to drive earnings deleverage.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financing terms for weaker borrowers: $120 billion of Oracle and SpaceX debt at 8.5% takes their combined interest coverage from 4.0x to 1.8x, and the article says the capex estimates depend on individual borrowers accessing capital on workable terms.

tension_points.bull_case: Memory stocks at about 3x NTM P/E, with the cycle late-stage by 4Q26 but not ending, and bottleneck pricing power across memory and HDDs.
tension_points.bear_case: Headline capex growth is partly a memory-price variable. In the 2022 NAND downturn shipments fell about 5% but prices fell 20-30%, and MS says volumes and prices falling together is underappreciated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Contract price growth slowing into 4Q26 and 2027 as MS expects would let hyperscalers report slower capex while building the same number of servers.

tension_points.bull_case: Power-solution providers are relative winners and the shortfall is a timing mismatch rather than a demand collapse per MS.
tension_points.bear_case: A 32 GW net US shortfall through 2028 (about 72 GW through 2029) means power-dependent equipment that cannot be turned on is hard to sustain buying, and memory, networking, optical and ODM builds are most exposed to a pause.

Free cash flow turns most negative in 2027 and weaker borrowers face thin interest coverage, so capital access may limit capex before demand does.
